item.title: Experimental demonstration of attosecond hard X-ray pulses
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 20 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02026-7 Researchers experimentally demonstrate attosecond pulse generation in the hard X-ray regime with a free-electron laser. The confirmation is enabled via the measurement of amplified spontaneous emission from 3d transition metals. Pulse durations are in the range of 100 as to 400 as.

item.title: Solution-processed nano-LEDs for next-generation optoelectronic technologies
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02010-1 This Review covers recent advances in quantum dots and perovskite nano-LEDs, discusses the challenge of balancing efficiency, stability and full-colour integration, and highlights potential future applications.

item.title: Ligand-engineered CsEuI<sub>3</sub> nanocrystals for efficient single-component white electroluminescence
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02039-2 Ligand-engineered CsEuI3 nanocrystals enable efficient single-component white electroluminescence with a peak external quantum efficiency of 8.3% and integration into active-matrix full-colour displays.

item.title: Quantum gates set speed record at 6.8 nanoseconds with over 99.98% accuracy
item.description: Researchers from Jülich, Aachen and Cologne have performed a quantum operation on a qubit in just 6.8 nanoseconds—with more than 99.98% accuracy. Such operations typically take several tens of nanoseconds in superconducting quantum computers. The paper was published in Nature Communications.

item.title: Intrinsic backward emission of coherent Raman photons from homogeneous media
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-01995-z Backscattered coherent Raman microscopy brings new opportunities.

item.title: Theoretical method uses light to locate anyons, potential quantum computing building blocks
item.description: Theoretical physicists at Emory University have discovered a way to use light to detect the "spectral fingerprints" of anyons—exotic quasiparticles that emerge from the collective behavior of many electrons. Their findings are published in Physical Review Letters. The work offers a new tool for the study of anyons, which hold potential as fundamental building blocks for quantum computing.

item.title: New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices using quantum mechanical effects, could potentially allow users to share information more securely and efficiently. Building these networks typically entails linking stationary qubits, units of quantum information encoded in trapped ions or other physical systems, using photons (particles of light) transmitted through optical fibers.

item.title: One extra quantum dot helps balance speed and stability in spin qubits
item.description: Quantum computers need qubits that can be controlled both quickly and reliably. Yet making semiconductor spin qubits faster often makes them more sensitive to electrical noise, creating a difficult trade-off.

item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it.
